entry.title: John Lewis marks 20th Christmas ad with star-studded effort

entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

John Lewis marks 20th Christmas ad with star-studded effort

Kristin Scott Thomas, Paul Whitehouse and Sam Fender feature in the retailer’s latest festive campaign, created by Saatchi & Saatchi, which combines traditional storytelling with a suitably theatrical finale

By Adam Woodward 03/11/2026 7:11 am

Has the John Lewis Christmas ad, which has been a much-anticipated fixture of the season since 2007, started to lose its lustre? Perhaps in anticipation of that question, the retailer has done something it has never done before at this time of year: put a bona fide star in front of the camera.

Fresh from her latest stint as the unflappable Diana Taverner in Slow Horses, Kristin Scott Thomas faces a prospect that would test the mettle of even the head of MI5: discontented grandkids. Whereas 2025’s ad focused on a father-son relationship, and 2024 put sisters at the fore, this year’s rather more traditional effort takes John Lewis’ ‘the home of thoughtful gifting’ proposition to its logical conclusion by centring on intergenerational gifting.

According to Saatchi & Saatchi, the initial idea was rooted in the insight that grandparents often feel unsure of what to get their grandchildren, and so simply resort to stuffing a few bank notes into a card. This is illustrated by Scott Thomas’ character, Gloria, venturing into her attic in search of a vintage toy she hopes will bring her two grandkids the same joy it once brought her (spoiler: it doesn’t).

For all that this year’s ad represents a first for the brand, however, it still contains many of the tried-and-trusted elements that viewers have come to expect. Chiefly, a twinkly a cappella cover of a classic song – if anyone had a children’s choir singing You Can’t Always Get What You Want on their bingo card, congratulations.

But there is more than meets the ear: as the song continues, Sam Fender’s stirring vocal kicks in and the ad shifts up a gear. As with the re-release of Where Love Lives in 2025, Fender’s version of the Rolling Stones’ late 60s hit will be available as a limited-edition vinyl, with all proceeds going to Action for Children as part of John Lewis’ Building Happier Futures initiative. There’s a nice personal touch to the recording, too: the children performing all belong to Fender’s old school choir.

But arguably the real star of the show is neither Fender nor Scott Thomas but another national treasure: Paul Whitehouse. Voicing a pull-along wooden dog named, for the purposes of this ad, Pickles, Whitehouse brings some much-needed irreverence to proceedings, his performance dovetailing neatly with Scott Thomas’ own. Each actor is aided by a script that complements their particular talents, while lines such as “Let’s go on a montage!” (Whitehouse) provide a knowing nod to the conventions of festive advertising.

Based on a Fisher-Price toy that has been sold since 1966, Pickles is unlikely to be this year’s must-have children’s toy, but it does serve as a fitting metaphor for feeling out of touch with the younger generation. Crucially, though, the ad doesn’t end with Gloria opting to follow the latest toy fad. Instead, after embarking on a tuk tuk ride through London with Pickles, she goes back into the attic to fetch some old furnishings that turn out to be rather more interesting. Cue a dramatic turn of a key and a genuine moment of wonder when the ‘gran cave’ is revealed in all its glittering, velvet-draped glory.

Directed by Lucy Forbes for Smuggler, the film has a cinematic sensibility that helps lift it above more familiar festive ad territory. The tuk tuk scene, in particular, brings to mind the similarly chaotic night bus ride at the start of Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban – a fitting touch from Forbes, who has just wrapped on the forthcoming HBO series.

More broadly, her direction gives the film a welcome sense of scale and theatricality, ensuring that its final reveal feels like a suitably magical payoff rather than simply another exercise in Christmas sentimentality or clunky product placement. It also appears that CR’s criticism of last year’s ad was taken on board, as the on-screen talent is notably more diverse than before.

The 20th edition of the John Lewis Christmas ad may not be an instant classic, then, but it makes a convincing case for keeping certain traditions alive while allowing others to evolve with the times.

entry.title: Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices Mother Design’s refresh transforms the psychic-services platform from a transactional experience into a calming space for long-term growth By Daniel Milroy Maher 03/11/2026 3:22 am Following Mother Desi
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices

Mother Design’s refresh transforms the psychic-services platform from a transactional experience into a calming space for long-term growth

By Daniel Milroy Maher 03/11/2026 3:22 am

Following Mother Design’s recent rebrand of spiritual guidance marketplace Keen, the agency has collaborated once again with its parent company Ingenio – this time on a rebrand of its other psychic services brand, Purple Garden. Whereas the Keen work aimed to entice a mainstream audience unfamiliar with spirituality, this project sees the brand appealing to ‘seasoned seekers’ instead.

Built around the creative concept of ‘A Living Practice’, the rebrand looks to reposition the platform from a destination for one-off readings to a site that facilitates long-term spiritual practice. For the team at Mother, embracing the intuition inherent in this kind of spiritual experience was key to reflecting Purple Garden’s offerings.

As such, they kicked off their creative process with a séance and chakra reading led by a Purple Garden holistic practitioner, followed by an automatic drawing and writing workshop that involved the designers working with charcoal on paper. The aim was for the team to bypass conscious thought and “step away from the screen and the rational design process”, says Mother Design creative director Joanna Tulej.

The forms, textures and feelings that emerged from this session became the raw material for the identity, drawing inspiration from artists such as Hilma af Klint and The Five, who used trance states and automatic drawing to allow imagery to surface naturally. Across Purple Garden’s assets, these organic elements are rendered using a mix of conventional design software and AI tools. The designers at Mother generated multiple iterations of the work to encourage unexpected results.

The typography follows a similar tone, revolving around a wordmark featuring elongated serifs and curved junctures that merges the modern with the whimsical. This is complemented by the typeface Literatura Present by Roman Gornitsky, with flowing descenders that add to the sense of growth, and the typeface ABC Social by Dinamo, which ensures usability on-screen.

Across the identity, the shades of purple that dominate the palette are offset by pink, maroon and grey, bringing a more dynamic feel to the aesthetic, but retaining the serene atmosphere associated with Purple Garden.

With the rebrand currently rolling out across web, advertising and social channels – soon to be followed by the app itself – Hellebuyck insists that the team at Mother “has created something that feels distinctive to Purple Garden and true to our audience, while giving us a richer and more immersive platform for the next stage of the brand”.

Finally, the Mother design team introduced “living type” to the identity, with enlarged words, inspired by cymatic patterns, which melt off the screen and reflect the way a phrase from a practitioner can stay with you and shape you long after the session has ended.

Elsewhere, imagery of objects with solarised glows and flame-like ripples depict services such as dream analysis and psychic readings, symbolising the energy passing between practitioner and customer. These are coupled with photographs that show intimate physical sensation, natural landscapes and organic textures, filtered through the brand’s purple hues to create the notion of an altered reality.

entry.summary: Creative Insight Creating desire in the face of climate catastrophe The climate crisis is deeply serious, but the way to engage audiences in sustainable brands doesn’t need to be – instead we should make the future feel like something worth buying into, says Ragged Edge’s Matt Sm
entry.content:
Creative Insight

Creating desire in the face of climate catastrophe

The climate crisis is deeply serious, but the way to engage audiences in sustainable brands doesn’t need to be – instead we should make the future feel like something worth buying into, says Ragged Edge’s Matt Smith

By Matt Smith 03/11/2026 3:02 am

The latest UN climate report makes for grim reading. The world is effectively committed to exceeding 1.5°C of global warming in the next few years. The question now is how far beyond that threshold we’ll go and whether we’ll figure out a way to pull back.

It’s a scary development. Yet with global instability and AI absorbing so much of our attention, climate change has slipped down our news feeds, even as its consequences become obvious. The climate crisis is fundamentally a systemic problem. Addressing it requires political will, regulation, infrastructure and investment on a scale that creative persuasion or individual choice can’t hope to deliver.

But consumer demand can encourage change, and branding is a tool designed to create it. For better and worse, we’re pretty good at making people want things. Yet when it comes to selling more sustainable products and services, we’ve spent a lot of time telling people what they ought to do, and not enough making them actually want to do it.

entry.title: Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot A misplaced grocery order, a broken-down car and an unexpected reunion provide the ingredients for Tesco’s latest Christmas ad by BBH London By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 10:12 am Created by BBH
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot

A misplaced grocery order, a broken-down car and an unexpected reunion provide the ingredients for Tesco’s latest Christmas ad by BBH London

By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 10:12 am

Created by BBH London, the three-minute film, The Wrong Address, tells a tale of reconnection and forgiveness, with much of the action playing out in a Tesco delivery van.

Starring Roisin Conaty as delivery driver Polly and Anna Maxwell Martin as her old school friend Lizzie, the pair cross paths after Lizzie accidentally sends her Christmas delivery to her old address.

Now living hundreds of miles apart, the pair arrange to meet halfway to retrieve the groceries. But when Lizzie’s car breaks down, Polly steps in to help, and the two embark on an unexpected journey back to Lizzie’s new home, reminiscing and slipping back into their old friendship with ease.

The ad ends with a heartwarming embrace and the line ‘Because this Christmas, Every Little Helps’, while The Police’s Every Little Thing She Does Is Magic plays in the background.

The film was directed by Steve Rogers through Biscuit Filmworks UK x Revolver, and the initial idea was sparked by Ioulianou’s own experience of accidentally ordering hangover food to the wrong address, in that case his nan’s house.

The Wrong Address marks a return to the hero film format for Tesco, in contrast to last year’s festive campaign, which featured 11 vignettes depicting relatable Christmas scenarios in a less sugar-coated take on the season.

This year, the knowing, slightly chaotic humour of last Christmas has been swapped for a more traditional festive formula, leaning into nostalgia, friendship and the emotional pull of a feel-good reunion.

entry.title: Richard Ayoade gets his Scrooge on for Argos Christmas ad
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Richard Ayoade gets his Scrooge on for Argos Christmas ad The comedian is spirited back to his youth courtesy of Connie the doll and Trevor the dinosaur in T&P’s latest spot for the retailer By Adam Woodward 02/11/2026 10:12 am British retailer Argos is build
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Richard Ayoade gets his Scrooge on for Argos Christmas ad

The comedian is spirited back to his youth courtesy of Connie the doll and Trevor the dinosaur in T&P’s latest spot for the retailer

By Adam Woodward 02/11/2026 10:12 am

British retailer Argos is building on its There’s More to Argos brand platform this holiday season with a playful twist on A Christmas Carol.

Created by T&P, Tales of Argos Past sees brand mascots Connie the doll and Trevor the dinosaur adopt the role of benevolent Christmas spirits to bring festive cheer (and a sackful of gift recommendations) to a Scrooge-like Richard Ayoade.

Directed by Declan Lowney (of Ted Lasso and Father Ted fame) through Merman, the ad transports viewers back to Ayoade’s childhood via the magic of grainy home video, where he sheds his curmudgeonly demeanour – but crucially not his natty corduroy suit and red knitted tie.

All told, it’s a fairly safe effort, and it must be said that Connie and Trevor’s shtick is starting to wear thin. It’s saved, however, by the fact that Ayoade is clearly having fun recreating moments from the novel, such as leaning out of a window to call out to a passerby; in this case an Argos delivery driver.

The product integration is nicely done, too – who else remembers circling their most sought-after items in the Argos catalogue? – and while CR is running a sweepstakes on how many of this year’s Christmas ads feature people wearing LED face masks, we’ll be surprised if any do so to better comic effect.

If nothing else, tapping into the cosy feeling of Christmas nostalgia makes perfect sense for a high street institution that has been around since 1973, but which has struggled more recently to shed its image as a glorified toy shop. Then again, Connie and Trevor’s continued presence rather does undermine the point.

When it comes to reminding consumers what this time of year is really all about, then, perhaps there is still life in the old Christmas classics. As Charles Dickens once said (probably): if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

entry.title: Sainsbury’s welcomes back the BFG for a festive adventure
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Sainsbury’s welcomes back the BFG for a festive adventure The supermarket has turned once again to the much-loved giant, this time taking viewers on an action-packed journey into Giant Country By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 9:22 am Created in partnership wi
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Sainsbury’s welcomes back the BFG for a festive adventure

The supermarket has turned once again to the much-loved giant, this time taking viewers on an action-packed journey into Giant Country

By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 9:22 am

Created in partnership with New Commercial Arts, this year’s Christmas ad for the supermarket opens with a poorly BFG announcing that he’ll be missing Christmas. Keen not to let her pal miss out, returning Sainsbury’s colleague Annie sets off on a daring mission to deliver a festive feast, embarking on a journey across Giant Country with delivery driver Fred.

Of course, the road to Christmas is far from straightforward. The Greedy Giant from last year’s instalment also makes a return, hell-bent on stopping the pair – at one point, he opens his gob so wide it’s nearly mistaken for a tunnel.

Along the way, Annie and Fred find themselves zooming through a patch of snozzcumbers, distracting an oversized Squizzly Scotch-Hopper with a plate of cheese, and unleashing an avalanche of Brussels sprouts to trip up their foe. Eventually, the pair make it to the BFG’s cave, where Annie arrives with crates of festive treats and a misty-eyed giant.

While wheeling the BFG out for a third time risks covering old ground for the brand, taking viewers into Giant Country does help counter that slightly, offering a change from the usual snowy streets of suburbia.

Alongside NCA, the spot was directed by Sam Brown and production was led by Rogue Films, with visual effects from Electric Theatre Collective bringing the fantastical world and its larger-than-life inhabitants to life.

The work builds on Sainsbury’s commitment to providing ‘Good food for all of us’. A special version of the ad will also highlight the retailer’s partnership with Comic Relief and its ambition to raise enough money to fund 12 million meals this year, supporting organisations across the UK helping children and families access good food.

entry.title: How brands are tackling health taboos
entry.summary: Creative Insight How brands are tackling health taboos Brands are using creativity to make difficult health subjects easier to discuss. CR explores how they can challenge stigma, open up new conversations and give audiences the confidence to take action By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/1
entry.content:
Creative Insight

How brands are tackling health taboos

Brands are using creativity to make difficult health subjects easier to discuss. CR explores how they can challenge stigma, open up new conversations and give audiences the confidence to take action

By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 7:53 am

There was a time when advertising preferred to keep the uncomfortable parts of being human out of sight. Menopause was euphemised or not acknowledged at all, weight loss was framed as a question of willpower, and conversations about libido, hormones and intimate health were largely confined to the doctor’s surgery – or avoided altogether.

That reluctance now feels out of step with modern life. Younger generations, social media and online communities have brought once-private experiences into public conversation, creating an appetite for brands willing to address them directly. More and more campaigns have tackled a range of health taboos, so now it’s about how creativity can offer new ways to make these subjects engaging, from musical theatre to animated Vikings.

But there is a tension at the heart of this movement. Brands can help people feel seen and encourage them to seek support. They can also sell products by persuading people that something about their bodies or lives needs fixing. When the audience is vulnerable, the distinction matters.

entry.title: Pablo London creates pork-based horror villain for PETA
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Pablo London creates pork-based horror villain for PETA The agency’s first campaign for the animal rights charity draws on slasher film tropes to highlight the link between processed meats and cancer By Adam Woodward 30/10/2026 12:33 pm It’s a classic trope o
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Pablo London creates pork-based horror villain for PETA

The agency’s first campaign for the animal rights charity draws on slasher film tropes to highlight the link between processed meats and cancer

By Adam Woodward 30/10/2026 12:33 pm

It’s a classic trope of horror films that often the most ordinary settings can conceal the most sinister threats. That’s the premise behind Pablo London’s new work for PETA, which turns processed meat into a character straight out of a John Carpenter slasher.

Arriving just in time for Halloween, the campaign introduces a grotesque antagonist named Hamface – all greasy skin and vacant grin – who is designed to make consumers reconsider the everyday foods they might otherwise give little thought to.

Rather than simply spoofing horror conventions, however, Pablo has opted for an enjoyably faithful homage that is positively dripping with dread. The result takes its cues from genre touchstones such as Halloween, but instead of a masked killer in the Michael Myers mould, an unsuspecting family are tormented by a giant slab of nondescript pork.

The similarly horror-inspired taglines which feature in the campaign film and accompanying posters are grounded in the World Health Organization’s classification of processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen, placing it in the same category as tobacco smoking and asbestos in terms of the strength of evidence that it causes cancer.

According to a 2015 estimate from the WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer, eating 50g of processed meat daily – roughly two slices of bacon – increases the relative risk of colorectal cancer by about 18%. As PETA notes, “eating a ham sandwich doesn’t scream danger … yet eating processed meat is linked to 34,000 cancer deaths globally every year”.

While PETA is best known for campaigning against animal cruelty, highlighting the risks to human health is a smart tactical choice. The film and its titular monster, which were brought to life by Riot directors Amy Fasey-Jones and Nathalie Gordon, in partnership with ArtClass, certainly provides audiences with a compelling reason to reconsider their habits, beyond the welfare of the animals involved.

Hamface marks Pablo London’s first campaign for PETA, and continues the charity’s use of provocative creative to promote veganism by looking beyond the obvious ethical arguments, following recent work linking plant-based diets with men’s health and a fecal-themed animated spot. The message here feels particularly apt for spooky season: this Halloween, the call is coming from inside the fridge.

entry.title: Energy drives Uncommon Creative Studio’s rebrand of White & Case
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Energy drives Uncommon Creative Studio’s rebrand of White & Case Built for a “hyper-complex world”, the Studio’s new identity for White & Case highlights how the firm responds to increasingly intricate work By Daniel Milroy Maher 30/10/2026 3:33 am Internatio
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Energy drives Uncommon Creative Studio’s rebrand of White & Case

Built for a “hyper-complex world”, the Studio’s new identity for White & Case highlights how the firm responds to increasingly intricate work

By Daniel Milroy Maher 30/10/2026 3:33 am

International law firm White & Case has partnered with Uncommon Creative Studio on a major new rebrand aimed at making the company stand out in the legal sector’s “sea of sameness”. Initiated by a new leadership team at the firm, this marks the first rebrand for White & Case in 13 years.

At the heart of the project is the notion of ‘complexity’, which increasingly characterises much of the firm’s work, and serves as the thematic foundation for Uncommon’s approach to the brief. Rather than shying away from complexity, White & Case is known for embracing it, and this can be seen across the firm’s new brand system.

“White & Case is a firm built for polycrisis,” explains Lisa Smith, global chief design officer at Uncommon. “They are high-stakes gladiators who step into friction when everyone else backs away.”

Beginning with the logo, Uncommon replaced White & Case’s old sans serif logotype with a custom one created to look like it was carved in ancient stone, taking inspiration from Trajan’s Column and Roman bedrock typography. Legible yet dynamic, the new wordmark imbues the visual language of the legal tradition with a markedly contemporary energy.

From this, the team at Uncommon crafted a striking monogram that combines the White & Case acronym with an “activated” ampersand, to “celebrate the power of global partnership”. At once playful and punchy, this symbol lives across many of the firm’s touchpoints, from its website to its social channels.

Uncommon also developed a series of powerful images for the identity that reflect White & Case’s energetic approach to complex issues. Using a proprietary tool called Energy Studio, the designers manipulated photographs of humans in motion to create “spotlit, kinetic vignettes”, as well as photographs of global infrastructure to cause them to bleed into “sharp, vertical streams of data”.

Finally, the design team carefully chose a spirited colour palette that could match and even enhance the already dynamic visuals. At the centre is the vibrant Catalyst Blue, taken from the highest-energy end of the visible light spectrum, which is offset by Marble White and Ink Black, and complemented by a secondary palette of shades called Ion, Thermal, Solar and Ultraviolet.

All of these design elements are brought to life in a two-minute anchor film titled The Power of Complexity, which features lively uses of motion design to showcase the new brand system. These unfold, fittingly, against an improvised jazz score that harmonises with the fast-paced visuals.

Reflecting on her team’s approach to the project, Smith says: “The legal sector is drowning in navy blue slabs, borrowing from tired financial and tech clichés, and safe choices… We built a dynamic, assertive identity that cuts through the noise, proving that design isn’t just about how a firm looks, but how it multiplies its force on the world stage.”

entry.summary: Creative Process Exposure: Marwan Bassiouni Bassiouni talks to Gem Fletcher about his striking photographic series, New Western Views, which depicts European landscapes through the windows of mosques By Gem Fletcher 30/10/2026 3:18 am In his long-term project New Western Views, M
entry.content:
Creative Process

Exposure: Marwan Bassiouni

Bassiouni talks to Gem Fletcher about his striking photographic series, New Western Views, which depicts European landscapes through the windows of mosques

By Gem Fletcher 30/10/2026 3:18 am

In his long-term project New Western Views, Marwan Bassiouni explores ways of seeing the Western landscape from an unexpected perspective: through the windows of mosques. By turning the camera outward from Muslim places of worship towards the surrounding landscape, he invites viewers to reconsider familiar environments from a different position and to reflect on how perspective and context shape the way we see.

The project — which currently traverses the UK, Netherlands, Switzerland, Canada and the United States of America — unravels an interconnected web of themes including belonging, spirituality and presence as well as national and collective identity.

“When I started making work in mosques, I was never specifically interested in architecture, or even in landscape,” Bassiouni explains when I ask him about the catalyst for the project. “I was interested in the subject. My intention from the beginning was to make work about the perception of Islam. Perception became this metaphysical subject matter, despite this topic always being framed in a politically charged way.”

entry.title: Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign Created by adam&eveTBWA, the work takes aim at tech billionaires’ apocalyptic tendencies while offering outdoor enthusiasts the chance to win a fully stocked bunker By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:53
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Columbia launches a Don’t Panic Room in latest campaign

Created by adam&eveTBWA, the work takes aim at tech billionaires’ apocalyptic tendencies while offering outdoor enthusiasts the chance to win a fully stocked bunker

By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:53 am

In recent years, Columbia Sportswear has become known for its tongue-in-cheek approach to outdoor advertising, often putting its gear to the test in deliberately absurd scenarios.

Its latest campaign, created by adam&eve\TBWA, centres around the Don’t Panic Room – a campaign and contest inviting audiences to showcase their survival skills for the chance to win a fully stocked, off-grid bunker equipped with Columbia gear and survival essentials.

Directed by Benji Weinstein and produced by Smuggler, the film takes aim at the “wealthy tech bros” preparing for the apocalypse in private bunkers, arguing that ordinary outdoor enthusiasts deserve a shot at survival, too.

Fronting the film is Columbia CEO Tim Boyle, whose appearances in previous campaigns, including last year’s open letter to Flat Earthers, have helped establish his place in the brand’s irreverent advertising. This time, he invites viewers to prove their survival skills, with the campaign imagining how Columbia’s gear could come in handy when the world takes a turn for the worse.

The campaign’s more playful touches include puffer jackets sealed in cans, dubbed “canned heat”, ready to be opened in an emergency. Featuring Columbia’s Omni-Heat Infinity thermal-reflective technology, the jackets bring a product-focused twist to the survivalist concept.

Of course the apparel is only part of the prize, the main draw is the 40ft-by-8ft modified shipping container that comes equipped with a kitchen, bathroom, bunk bed and survival supplies, as well as a robotic dog named Rocky.

“The Don’t Panic Room is the perfect embodiment of Columbia’s brand platform, Engineered For Whatever, celebrating the ingenuity, irreverence and spirit of adventure that define the brand,” says Ant Nelson, chief creative officer at adam&eve\TBWA.

The campaign launched on social media, alongside a print ad in the New York Times and billboards across Silicon Valley, poking fun at the tech elite’s obsession with preparing for disaster. Entries are open until the end of November, with participants able to submit videos showcasing their outdoor survival skills via Instagram or Columbia’s website.

entry.title: The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford
entry.summary: Creative Insight The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford DoorDash’s ECD reflects on leaving the agency world behind, the art of building strong partnerships, and how everyday human truths drive the brand’s most creative work By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:30 am Kirsten Ruth
entry.content:
Creative Insight

The Monthly Interview: Kirsten Rutherford

DoorDash’s ECD reflects on leaving the agency world behind, the art of building strong partnerships, and how everyday human truths drive the brand’s most creative work

By Rebecca Fulleylove 29/10/2026 3:30 am

Kirsten Rutherford’s first experience of advertising involved a sugar rush and a room full of rainbow markers. Her father was managing director of Leo Burnett Auckland, and while he worked weekends, she would run wild through the creatives’ offices, drawing with their marker pens and leaving the lids off, all the while drinking Sprite (one of the agency’s clients). “Those poor art directors would come in on Monday to discover their very expensive tools had dried out,” she tells CR. “But I remember being incredibly happy there.”

By the age of eight, Rutherford had already decided she wanted to be a copywriter. Decades later, after a career spanning New Zealand, London and the US, and agencies including TBWA\Chiat\Day, Team One, 72andSunny and Wieden+Kennedy, she has taken her curiosity about creativity to the other side of the business. At the beginning of 2026, she joined DoorDash as executive creative director, leading its in-house creative studio, Superette.

The move was driven by a desire to get closer to the problems behind the advertising. “I’d had offers from brands before, but DoorDash was the first that shared my creative ambition,” she says. “It’s a business full of fascinating problems, with a seriously talented creative crew. It was an easy yes.” For the creative, being inside the business means spotting opportunities before they become briefs and seeing how creativity can answer real business problems.

Top: In Case of Emergency campaign; Above: Order, Delivered campaign; © DoorDash

At 17, while finishing high school, Rutherford responded to a creative brief in a national newspaper for the Axis Idea School, a night course run by New Zealand’s leading agencies. She was one of 12 people selected, and much younger than most of her classmates. “There were university graduates and people coming from all sorts of different careers and walks of life,” she says. “One of the best creatives I know came through the course having been a sheep farmer, which is very Kiwi.”

The course gave her the beginnings of a portfolio and led to an internship at DDB. She was studying marketing at university when M&C Saatchi offered her a copywriting job after her first semester. She took it, and never completed her degree. “So I still don’t have a degree, but I’ve managed to find my way creatively around the world.”

Much of Rutherford’s career has been shaped by the places she’s lived in, and moving between countries taught her to question her assumptions. “What’s funny, what’s obvious, what people care about – you have to learn all of that again. It teaches you to listen,” she says.

New Zealand gave her resourcefulness and “a healthy lack of preciousness”; London sharpened her appreciation for craft, while America expanded her sense of what was possible. Her experiences across different agencies also helped shape her approach to leadership. “People do their best work when they feel equally challenged and supported,” she says. “When they can feel safe enough to share something unhinged or unfinished and trust that everyone wants to make it better.”

DoorDash has a lovely connection to real life: what people need, what they crave, what they’ve forgotten, what might make their day a little better

At DoorDash, Superette’s remit spans creative work for Consumer, Dasher and Merchant audiences, stewardship of the brand’s voice and design, and partnerships supporting its Ads Platform, co-marketing, and growth partners. Working closely with teams across strategy, social, operations, marketing, growth and insights gives the studio a close understanding of the business and the people it serves.

A recent example is Order, Delivered, a campaign that finds creative possibility in everyday chaos. Using a DoorDash delivery photo as a starting point, the films reveal the stories behind the orders, from new parents whose plans are derailed by a nappy emergency to a sleep-deprived mother ordering postpartum essentials like formula, nipple cream, ice cream and a robot vacuum.

The situations are specific but relatable. “Our Order, Delivered work shows how much creative possibility there is in paying attention to those everyday truths,” Rutherford says. “DoorDash has a lovely connection to real life: what people need, what they crave, what they’ve forgotten, what might make their day a little better. There’s an enormous amount of human behaviour to be curious about.”

The In Case Of campaign, developed in partnership with Gut, takes that thinking in a different direction. Reimagining the familiar emergency box, it explores DoorDash’s ability to deliver almost anything in almost any situation, from bandages for runners experiencing chafing during a marathon to baseball gloves in case of foul balls at Wrigley Field.

“The fun comes from where those boxes show up, what’s inside and why you might need it,” Rutherford says. “The connection between the situation and the object makes the idea work.”

The brand’s wider collaborations this year span equally varied territory. With MikeTeeVee, Superette developed Don’t Fan for Free, a football campaign featuring Bill Belichick as the brand’s Fan Coach, and It’s All in the Delivery, starring New York Knicks player Josh Hart.

Our internal team has a closeness to the business that brings depth. Our agency partners have a little distance, which allows them to bring equal passion, but a different perspective

Other projects – while not led by Superette – similarly round out the picture of the brand’s creative landscape. Loop, for instance, recently helped create CringeMart, a humorous in-app storefront for life’s most awkward purchases, supported by hidden-camera films and live condom-counter billboards. Wieden+Kennedy Toronto’s Not That Dramatic took a cinematic approach to the everyday dilemma of ordering dinner.

For Rutherford, knowing when to bring in external partners is part of balancing creative ambition with commercial demands. “Our internal team has a closeness to the business that brings depth. Our agency partners have a little distance, which allows them to bring equal passion, but a different perspective.”

The decision depends on the problem, the expertise required and where a partner could strengthen the work. What matters is establishing clear responsibilities and a relationship in which people can challenge one another without becoming territorial. “I want our partners to feel close enough to the business to understand it, and trusted enough to challenge us.”

Rutherford’s belief in collaboration extends far beyond daily agency operations – it has also opened doors for creativity to make a broader social impact. Sometimes those opportunities stem directly from long-standing relationships.

After working with CMO Janell Holas on a detergent brand, Rutherford stayed in touch long after the account ended. When Holas later took the helm as CMO of Make-A-Wish, that connection allowed Rutherford to lend her creative support to the organisation’s mission on several occasions.

Other times, the connection is deeply personal. While at TBWA\Chiat\Day, she leapt at the chance to work on Gatorade’s Sisters in Sweat, a campaign encouraging young girls to stay involved in sports. Having taught group exercise for years, the topic hit close to home.

“I know first-hand what movement can give you, so I really wanted to be involved,” she says. “I wrote a letter for Serena Williams to read to her newborn daughter, and it was a joy to see Sisters in Sweat come to life.”

Exploring what girls gain from sport – and what they stand to lose when they drop out – exemplifies for Rutherford how creativity can spotlight experiences that deserve recognition. It also served as a reminder of how easily leaders can mistake their own background for a universal truth.

“Your own experience is just one perspective,” she notes. “The people around the table will see things you don’t, if you simply give them the room to contribute.” She wants to see greater transparency around progression in the creative industries, broader routes into creative roles and more active sponsorship of people whose work deserves to be seen. “Representation needs to come with influence and opportunity. Leaders need to look honestly at who is getting both, and take responsibility for changing that.”

Having entered advertising through the Axis Idea School, Rutherford understands the importance of opening doors. She believes that emerging talent needs useful feedback, meaningful opportunities and the confidence to develop their own voice. “We can be rigorous about an idea while helping someone understand that feedback on the work isn’t a verdict on their talent or their future,” she says.

Her advice to creatives progressing into leadership is to stay curious about the work and the people around it, without losing enthusiasm for the craft. “Look at things, talk about ideas, care about the details. Be a ridiculously overexcited ad nerd,” she says.

“Don’t be afraid to share your enthusiasm for whatever weird subculture brings you joy (even if that means rave music, old rescue dogs, drag and cake). Enthusiasm is infectious, and it matters even more when you’re leading.”

As Rutherford sees it, leadership is about learning to take satisfaction in helping others make something brilliant. It means creating the conditions for people to do their best work and leaving room for them to surprise you. For someone whose earliest memories of an agency involved being given the freedom to draw all over the place, it feels like a fitting philosophy.
